match.reason: No point in the bank covers the limits of financial reports; the closest ones, such as profit and monitoring performance, are related ideas but do not teach how reports can hide problems.

draft.title: Limits of financial reports
card: Financial reports follow accounting rules, but managers still make choices inside those rules. Some choices can make a business look healthier than it is.
Normalised earnings
profit adjusted to remove items seen as one-off, so it shows usual performance. If real costs are removed too often, profit looks higher than it was.
Capitalised expense
a cost recorded as an asset instead of an expense. Expenses reduce profit straight away, so capitalising a cost lifts profit for now.
Valuing assets
assets rely on estimates, such as what a building or stock is worth. An overvalued asset makes the business look stronger. Debts left out of a report, or reported late, can hide problems too.
draft.remember: A report is only as honest as the choices and estimates behind its figures.

a.q: A firm records the cost of a major repair as an asset instead of an expense. What is the effect on this year's profit?
opts: Profit looks higher than if it was an expense
Profit looks lower than if it was an expense
Profit is unchanged, as the cash paid is the same
Profit looks higher because the firm earned more sales
a.why: An expense cuts profit straight away, but an asset does not. Recording the repair as an asset lifts profit for now. The cash paid is the same, but profit is not, so the unchanged option is wrong.
a.clue: Which of the two, an expense or an asset, reduces profit straight away?

b.q: Dana is thinking of buying Harbour Hardware. Its report shows strong profit, but she learns that the owner values old stock at far above what it could sell for. Which is the best description of the risk?
opts: Overvalued assets make the business look stronger than it is
Undervalued assets make the business look weaker than it is
Stock values are fixed by law so the report is reliable
Strong profit proves the business has no hidden debts
b.why: Stock valued above what it could sell for is an overvalued asset, which makes the business look stronger. A strong profit figure does not show that debts are fully reported, so the last option is tempting but wrong.
b.clue: Think about what an inflated asset value does to how strong the business looks.

a.best: Profit looks higher than if it was an expense

b.best: Overvalued assets make the business look stronger than it is

problems.detail: The why calls the 'no hidden debts' option 'the last option'. Options appear in random order, and here the last option shown is the correct one ('Overvalued assets...'). Students would read the why as calling the right answer wrong. Name the option by its content, not its position.

The sentence about debts left out of a report or reported late sits inside the 'Valuing assets' bullet, so it reads as part of asset valuation. The chapter treats timing of issues and omitted debts as separate limits, so this is confusing.

proposal.title: Limits of financial reports
card: Normalised earnings
profit adjusted to remove items seen as one-off, so it shows usual performance. If real costs are removed too often, profit looks higher than it was.
Capitalised expense
a cost recorded as an asset instead of an expense. Expenses reduce profit straight away, so capitalising a cost lifts profit for now.
Valuing assets
assets rely on estimates made by managers, such as what a building or stock is worth. An overvalued asset makes the business look stronger than it is.
Timing of issues: income or costs can be recorded in a different period to make one year look better. Separately, debts left out of a report hide how much is owed.
proposal.remember: A report is only as honest as the choices and estimates behind its figures.
